n: Dated June 587 BC, this oracle uses an allegory of a great tree to warn Pharaoh.

f.w: in the eleventh year, in the third month, in the first day

n: God asks Pharaoh: Who are you like in your greatness? Consider a lesson from history.

f.w: Whom art thou like in thy greatness?
f.g: A rhetorical question setting up the comparison.

n: Assyria was once like a towering cedar of Lebanon with beautiful branches and shade, its top among the clouds. Yet Assyria had fallen in 612–609 BC.

f.w: the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon
f.g: Some scholars read “cypress” instead of “Assyria,” making the tree itself Egypt; either way, the fall of a great empire is the lesson.

f.w: shadowing shroud

n: Deep waters nourished it, and streams flowed around it to all the trees of the field—the empire’s wealth and power.

f.w: the deep set him up on high
f.g: Underground waters made it grow tall.

n: So it grew taller than every other tree, with spreading branches.

f.w: his height was exalted above all the trees

n: Birds nested in its boughs, animals bore young beneath it, and great nations lived in its shade—the empire sheltered many peoples.

f.w: All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs

n: It was magnificent because its roots reached abundant water.

f.w: his root was by great waters

n: Even the trees in Eden, God’s garden, could not rival it.

f.w: the garden of God
chestnut trees

n: God made it beautiful—its glory was a gift—and all Eden’s trees envied it.

f.w: I have made him fair

n: But because it grew proud of its height, its heart was lifted up.

f.w: his heart is lifted up in his height

n: So God handed it to a mighty ruler of the nations—Babylon—who dealt with it as its wickedness deserved.

f.w: the mighty one of the heathen
f.g: Nebuchadnezzar or the Babylonian-Median alliance that defeated Assyria.

n: Ruthless foreigners cut it down. Its branches lie across mountains and valleys, and the nations abandon its shade.

f.w: the terrible of the nations

n: Birds and beasts now sit on its fallen trunk and branches—where they once found shelter, now they find a carcass.

f.w: Upon his ruin

n: The lesson: no tree, however well-watered, should exalt itself. All are destined for death, going down to the pit like ordinary mortals.

f.w: the nether parts of the earth
f.g: The underworld, the realm of the dead.

f.w: they are all delivered unto death

n: When it fell, God made the deep mourn and the waters stop; Lebanon and all trees grieved. Its fall affected the whole world.

f.w: I caused a mourning

n: The nations shook at its fall as God cast it down to Sheol. The other fallen trees of Eden were comforted to see the mighty one join them.

f.w: hell
f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, the realm of the dead, not necessarily a place of punishment.

f.w: shall be comforted

n: Its allies who lived in its shade went down to Sheol with it.

f.w: they that were his arm

n: Now God applies the lesson: Pharaoh, which tree in Eden are you like? You too will be brought down to lie among the uncircumcised and the slain. “This is Pharaoh.”

f.w: This is Pharaoh and all his multitude
f.g: The allegory is applied directly to Egypt.

f.w: in the midst of the uncircumcised
